headline: Gators at the Hook, Fluke Riding Shotgun on the Reefs Behind Them
subhead: Bunker got run down off Sandy Hook Friday and the blues that did it are still around — here's where I'm putting the boat this week.
body_markdown:
I made the call Thursday night to skip the back bay entirely this week and run straight for the Hook, and Friday told me I was right before I even had a line in the water. Bunker schools that had been holding off Keyport and up in the flats got pushed tight to the beach on the ocean side of the Hook, and the blues that found them turned it into a real blitz — gators busting bait on the surface right where the sand meets the deep water off the Rip. I said last week that blues would build here as that wave from the north filled in, and that's exactly what happened. No mystery to it: warm bay water in August pushes stripers and bait out toward the cooler edge current at the Hook, and the bluefish follow the bunker right to the beach.

Here's the thing though — this isn't a bay story right now, it's a Hook story. Raritan Bay proper, the flats off Keyport, the Highlands side — that's been a slog. Water's warm, current's soft on the small tides, and the stripers that are still around are hunkered in the deeper holes and not moving much until the sun's off the water. I said it last week and I'll say it again: this zone doesn't really turn over until water starts cooling toward September, and nothing this week changed my mind on that. If you're grinding the flats for bass right now expecting a spring-style bite, you're going to be disappointed. Save that gas.

What I am doing is working the Rip at the Hook on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, when the current is ripping hardest against that bottom structure. Bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounce, white or chartreuse, cast up-current and let them swing down through the seam where you can see the color change and the bait balling up. When the blues are actively busting on top I'll switch over to poppers or metal — a Hopkins or an Ava 27 with a single hook, because in a blitz like that you don't need finesse, you need something that gets down through the chop fast and comes back through the strike zone. Fights are short and violent, teeth everywhere, so bring a pair of long-nose pliers and don't put your fingers near the gill plate unless you enjoy stitches.

Fluke are the other piece of this that's actually worth your gas money. The reefs and snags just off the Hook on the ocean side have been quietly improving as that same warm bait push shoves smaller forage up onto the structure. I'm dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the edges of the reef in 25 to 35 feet, slow enough that you feel the bottom tick but fast enough to keep off the rocks. Best window has been the last of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, when the water's still moving but not screaming, and you can hold a controlled drift instead of getting blown through the zone. Nothing gigantic — most fish are 17 to 20 inches — but it's a real bite, and it's a lot more consistent right now than anything happening on the bay-side channel edges, which have gone quiet with the heat.

Porgies are still there if you want an easy box of fish for the table. Romer Shoal and the shallower stretches of Flynn's Knoll are holding scup in decent numbers on bottom rigs with pieces of clam or sandworm, fished right on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the slower part of either tide. It's not exciting fishing but it's dependable, and it's a good option for a family trip when the wind won't cooperate for anything more technical.

Weakfish I'll be honest with you — they're basically a non-factor in the bay right now. A few stragglers get picked up incidentally by fluke guys working soft plastics near the channel edges in the Navesink, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them in August. If you want weakfish, this isn't the month.

Looking ahead, the tidal range is building toward the new moon on the 12th, and that's the piece I'm watching closest. Bigger swings mean harder-running current at structure-driven spots like the Rip and the deeper cuts along the Hook, and that usually sharpens everything — bait gets pinned tighter, predators commit harder, and the bite windows get more defined even if they're shorter. If that plays out the way I expect, I'd look for the blitz activity at the Hook to intensify rather than fade over the next few days, and the fluke bite on the reef edges should hold or even improve as more current moves through. My plan is simple: hit the Rip on the moving water, work the reef drift on the slower stretches, and leave the bay flats alone until the heat breaks. If the wind stays out of the southwest and the bunker keep holding tight to that beach, there's no reason to be anywhere else.
